sections.plain_explanation:
Article 90 explains how the Code is organized, and 90.3 draws a line around Chapter 8. In plain terms, the general rules in Chapters 1 through 7 do not automatically apply to a communications installation. They apply only where Chapter 8 itself points back to them, or where a specific article in this chapter says so. That is why a rule you know well from power wiring cannot simply be carried over to a phone, data, or coax job. The reach-backs Chapter 8 actually makes include:
• 250.94 — the intersystem bonding termination that communications grounding lands on
• 300.4(D) and 300.11 — pulled in by 800.24 for protecting and supporting cable
• 300.22 — the air-handling space rules the chapter's cable rules reference
sections.why_it_exists: Crews carry habits from one system to another, and the wrong habit cuts both ways: it over-builds a comm job with power rules nobody asked for, or it skips a protection that Chapter 8 does require because the power article was never opened. The 90.3 line keeps every system judged by its own rules, and it tells you exactly where to look when the two worlds touch.
sections.on_the_job: When a power-wiring rule and a Chapter 8 job seem to collide, do not assume the power rule wins. Open the communications article first and look for a reference back to Chapters 1 through 7. On a Marion Oaks rough-in the crew argued over whether the 1¼ in stud-boring rule reaches a coax run. It does — not because Chapter 3 reaches across, but because 800.24 points to 300.4(D). If Chapter 8 is silent, ask the lead or the AHJ instead of inventing a bridge.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer: all of Chapter 3 applies to communications work because the cables run through the same studs. Wrong. Under 90.3, Chapters 1 through 7 apply to a Chapter 8 installation only where Chapter 8 specifically references them — the reference is the bridge, not the shared wall cavity.

sections.title: Article 800 — General requirements for communications systems
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 800 is the general article for communications systems, and it was new in the 2020 edition. Before 2020, almost every communications article repeated the same housekeeping rules in its own pages. Article 800 gathers them and states them once:
• Mechanical execution of work, and how cable is supported
• Abandoned cable — what has to come out
• Fire and smoke spread: firestopping, and cable listed for the space
• Cables entering a building, and protection at the entrance
• Bonding and grounding of protectors, sheaths and entrance hardware
• Separation from electric light and power conductors
• Cable listing and marking
Those general rules then apply to the specific systems in Articles 805, 820, 830 and 840, unless one of those articles changes them. Article 810, antennas, is the exception: it stands apart from Article 800 and carries its own rules.
sections.on_the_job: Read Article 800 first on any communications job, then read the specific article for the system you are installing. On a Winter Park office rough-in, the Cat 6, the coax and the broadband drops all enter at one demarc wall — one bonding point, one firestopping standard and one separation rule cover all three, because all three sit under Article 800. Most inspection failures Sharma would hit in this chapter — no bond at the entrance, cable mixed with power, dead cable left in a ceiling — are Article 800 failures, not failures of the specific system article.

NEC 2023 applies in Florida only to permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026 (FBC 9th Ed.), so until then a 2023 study book may show different Chapter 8 numbering or wording.
sections.why_it_exists: Communications work fails in the same handful of ways no matter which system is on the truck — a missing bond, a cable run with power, dead cable left in a ceiling. Stating the rule once means every system inherits the same floor, and an installer who learns the entrance, bonding and separation rules once can walk onto any communications job in the chapter already knowing most of what the inspector will check.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is assuming Article 800 covers everything in Chapter 8 the same way. It does not reach Article 810: antennas stand alone, with their own grounding recipe at 810.21. The second trap is reading only the system article — general duties like removing abandoned cable live in Article 800 and are easy to miss if you never open it.

sections.title: Scope of the general article
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 800 is the general article for Chapter 8. It states the requirements every communications system in the chapter shares, and it works together with the specific articles, so a telephone circuit, a CATV coax run, and a broadband entrance all start here for their shared rules.
• 800 — the general rules themselves
• 805 — communications circuits
• 810 — radio and television equipment
• 820 — community antenna television (CATV) coaxial systems
• 830 — network-powered broadband systems
• 840 — premises-powered broadband systems
Article 800 does not cover the utility's own plant under the utility's exclusive control, which Article 90 leaves outside the Code. The customer's side of the demarcation point is where this book's work lives.
sections.why_it_exists: Most Chapter 8 arguments on a job are really scope arguments: whose cable is it, and whose rules judge it? If the line between the provider's plant and the customer's wiring is fuzzy, the protector, the bonding and the separation work can fall between two crews, with each side sure the other one owns it. 800.1 draws the line so the entrance gets built once, by the crew the Code actually covers.
sections.on_the_job: On a service call at a Winter Park home, find the demarcation point first — the provider's box on the side of the house. Everything on the customer side is fair game for Chapter 8 rules; the provider's network on the other side is theirs. When the provider's installer and Sharma's crew disagree about a bond or a cable, this scope line usually settles whose rules apply: Sharma bonds the protector and runs the inside Cat 6 and coax, and the buried drop on the street side of the demarc stays the provider's problem.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer is that Article 800 covers telephone circuits only. It is the general article for the whole chapter — its rules ride on top of CATV, broadband and radio/TV work too. The reverse trap also shows up: applying Article 800 to the utility's own plant under its exclusive control, which the Code does not cover at all.

sections.title: Definitions that belong to this chapter
sections.plain_explanation:
Some words in this chapter carry Code definitions, and this section holds the ones communications work turns on. Two do daily duty:
• Point of entrance: the point where a communications wire or cable comes into the building from outside — through a wall, a floor, or a grounded metal raceway that extends it.
• Abandoned communications cable: cable that is not terminated at equipment and is not identified for future use with a tag.
Almost every entrance rule in the chapter is measured from the point of entrance, and the abandoned-cable definition is the test 800.25 then applies.
sections.on_the_job: Before arguing about where a protector, bond, or 50 ft limit lands, settle where the point of entrance is — the wall penetration, or the end of the grounded entrance conduit if one extends it. And when a dead cable is disputed, run the definition: terminated, or tagged for future use? If neither, it is abandoned.

sections.why_it_exists: Definitions are where inspections are won and lost. Measure the 50 ft allowance for unlisted outside-plant coax from the panel instead of from the point of entrance and the run is over the limit before anyone checks. Argue "abandoned" from the everyday meaning instead of the definition and dead cable stays in the ceiling. The definition is the measuring stick every other rule in the chapter is cut with.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer puts the point of entrance where the cable lands on the panel. Wrong — it is where the cable enters the building, and when a grounded metal raceway extends the entrance, the point moves to the end of that raceway. Measure the protector, the bond and the 50 ft from the wrong point and every one of them can fail.

Primary protector placed well inside the building because the entrance point was never settled.
Dead cable left in place as "not abandoned" — unterminated and untagged.
Cable marked "spare" in pen on the jacket, no durable tag — claimed as identified for future use.

sections.title: How Article 800 works with the other articles
sections.plain_explanation: Article 800 is a layer, not a replacement. Its general rules apply across the communications articles unless a specific article modifies them, and other NEC articles apply to a communications job only where Chapter 8 references them. One practical example: reconditioned communications equipment is pulled back to the general marking rules of Chapter 1 through this section. Another is grounding: Chapter 8 repeatedly sends you to the intersystem bonding termination described in 250.94, instead of restating it. So the order of work is always the same: general rule first, specific article second, referenced article only where the chapter points.
sections.on_the_job: A Kissimmee office rough-in mixes three Chapter 8 systems in one ceiling: 805 circuits for the phone system, 820 coax for the TV drops, and 830 broadband at the demarc. Work the layers in order on each one: 800 for the general rule, the specific article (805, 820, 830, or 840) for anything that changes it, then any article Chapter 8 points you to. Do not skip straight to a Chapter 3 wiring method and assume it governs a communications cable.

sections.why_it_exists: Chapter 8 systems carry signals, not building power, and their hazards are different — surge energy at entrances, fire spread along cable jackets, abandoned cable adding fuel. If every power-wiring rule in the earlier chapters applied by default, the communications articles would drown in exceptions. The layer design keeps one general rulebook for all communications work, lets each system article adjust it, and borrows an outside rule only by name.

sections.title: Keep the ceiling panels removable — cable cannot block access
sections.plain_explanation:
Access to electrical equipment must not be denied by an accumulation of communications wires and cables that prevents removal of panels, including suspended-ceiling panels. In plain terms, the tiles of a suspended ceiling are an access door to the junction boxes, disconnects, and other electrical equipment above them. A bundle of data cable draped across the grid so that a panel cannot be lifted out fails this section, even if every cable in the bundle is the right type, properly supported, and properly bonded. The rule is not about the cable — it is about keeping the access the ceiling was designed to give.
• The tiles of a suspended ceiling are access panels, not a shelf.
• Cable above the ceiling has to be routed and supported so the panel under the equipment can still come out.
sections.on_the_job: Tenant build-out in an Orlando office: forty Cat 6A drops for one suite. Route and support the runs so any ceiling panel can still be lifted and slid aside — bundles on their own hangers or J-hooks above the grid, never resting on the tiles, never piled across the panel below a box or disconnect someone will need to reach. If you cannot lift the tile, neither can the next electrician — and the inspector will try the tile nearest the equipment.

sections.title: Doing the work neatly and protecting the cable
sections.figure_idea: A photo-style drawing of a stud bay with a centered bored hole, a supported Cat 6 and coax run, and a red X over a cable zip-tied to an EMT run.
sections.plain_explanation:
This section requires communications work to be done in a neat, workmanlike way, and it ties cable installation to basic protection against physical damage.
• Circuits and equipment are installed in a neat and workmanlike manner — sloppy low-voltage work is still a code violation even though the voltage is low.
• Cables installed exposed on ceilings and sidewalls are supported by the building structure so normal building use cannot damage them, secured with straps, staples, cable ties, hangers or similar fittings that do not damage the cable.
• The installation also conforms to 300.4(D) — cable run through or parallel to framing keeps 1¼ in from the edge of the wood member, or gets a steel plate — and to 300.11 on securing and supporting.
• Nonmetallic cable ties and accessories used in plenum spaces must be listed as having low smoke and heat release properties.
Cables must never hang off other systems: not a power raceway, not a sprinkler pipe, not a ceiling grid wire that is not part of the support system.
sections.why_it_exists: Low voltage fools people into thinking the work cannot hurt anyone, so it gets draped, pinched and abandoned in ceilings. Then a drywall screw nicks the jacket, a ceiling tile change saws through an unsupported run, and the phone, data or alarm path the building counts on is dead — sometimes silently, until the day it is needed. Neat, supported, protected cable is what survives the other trades.
sections.on_the_job: Roughing in a three-bedroom home in Marion Oaks: dress the runs, support them on their own supports, and keep holes centered in studs the way you would for power cable — 1¼ in or more from the stud edge on 14 Cat 6 and coax home runs. Never hang a communications cable from a power raceway, a sprinkler pipe, or a ceiling grid wire that is not part of the support system. The one run a helper zip-tied to a sprinkler line on this job got cut and re-pulled before insulation. A neat rough-in is also the fastest one to inspect.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer is that a communications cable may rest on the ceiling grid and tie to the grid wires, because it is 'only low voltage.' Wrong twice: 800.24 sends support to 300.11, and the grid is not a cable support unless it is part of an identified support system. The voltage on the cable does not soften the mechanical rules.

sections.title: Abandoned cable has to come out
sections.plain_explanation:
A communications cable that is no longer terminated at equipment, and is not tagged for future use, counts as abandoned cable — the definition is in 800.2. The rule here:
• The accessible portion of abandoned cable must be removed.
• A cable you honestly plan to reuse may stay, but only if it carries a durable tag identifying it for future use, suited to the environment it sits in.
• Cable hidden inside a concealed raceway is not treated as accessible, so the removal duty reaches only what a crew can actually get to.
Dead cable is fuel in a ceiling or shaft, and it confuses every crew that comes later.
sections.on_the_job: On a remodel or a tenant finish-out, walk the ceiling before you add anything. On a Winter Park office finish-out we pulled roughly 300 ft of dead coax and old phone cable out of one ceiling before the new Cat 6 went in. Tag any spare you are keeping with what it is and where it goes — "future use, spare to the Suite 210 panel" — not a strip of tape. "We might use it someday" with no tag does not count.

sections.why_it_exists: Abandoned cable is jacket and insulation with no job to do. Above a ceiling it adds fuel and smoke load exactly where fire spreads unseen, and in a shaft it can carry flame from floor to floor. It also lies to the next crew: a toner finds a "live" pair that goes nowhere, a panel fills with ports that serve nothing, and a remodel bid quietly includes demo nobody priced.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is "all abandoned cable must come out, everywhere." The duty stops at the accessible portion: cable abandoned inside a concealed raceway is not accessible, and the Code does not make you open walls to chase it. The other wrong answer is the untagged spare — no durable tag, no future use, and the cable is abandoned by definition.

sections.title: Slowing the spread of fire and smoke
sections.plain_explanation:
Communications cables, raceways, and cable routing assemblies must be installed so they do not noticeably increase how fire or the products of combustion can spread through hollow spaces, shafts, and air-handling paths.
• Where a cable or raceway passes through a fire-resistance-rated wall, floor, partition, or ceiling, the opening around it has to be firestopped with an approved method that restores the rating.
• The firestop has to match the assembly and the cable type — a listed system, putty, or collars made for that penetration.
This mirrors the general firestopping rule in Chapter 3 (300.21), restated here because Chapter 8 stands on its own.
sections.on_the_job: Every poke through a rated assembly gets firestopped — putty, collars, or a listed system matched to the cable type and the assembly. On a Florida retail buildout, a bundle of two dozen Cat 6 and four coax through a 1-hour corridor wall gets a listed firestop system sized for that bundle, not a smear of caulk. Do not leave an oversized hole stuffed with scrap insulation and call it done. In Florida commercial work this is one of the most common communications corrections on a final inspection.

sections.title: Never run a cable hotter than its rating
sections.plain_explanation:
No wire or cable may be used in a way that makes its operating temperature exceed the temperature rating of the wire or cable. It is a one-sentence general rule — the Chapter 8 counterpart of the temperature limits the rest of the Code puts on conductors.
The heat it guards against can come from anywhere:
• The space itself — a hot attic, a boiler room, or a sun-baked exterior run.
• The cable's own load — communications cables that deliver power to devices warm up from the inside.
• The bundle — the middle of a fat bundle of powered cables warms up most, because its heat has nowhere to go.
The cable types in 800.179 are built around temperature: suitable for at least 60°C, with any higher rating marked on the cable. This section is the installation rule that says the rating has to be respected in the field, not just on the reel.
sections.on_the_job: Florida attic in July: the air at the roof deck is already hot before any current flows, and a PoE switch feeding cameras and access points puts real load on every pair in the bundle. Split the home runs into two smaller bundles instead of one fat one, keep them low in the attic and out of the insulation where the layout allows, and never strap a powered bundle against a flue or a recessed luminaire housing. If a design truly needs one big powered bundle, that is a design conversation — not a field shortcut.

sections.why_it_exists: Heat ages insulation. A jacket run past its rating turns brittle and cracks, and a bundle cooking from the inside can degrade for years above a ceiling before anyone sees it. The first symptom is usually intermittent data faults on the hottest runs; the end of the story is a cable plant that has to be replaced.

sections.title: Overhead wires and cables coming into a building
sections.plain_explanation:
Overhead communications wires and cables that enter a building have clearance and separation rules where they cross roofs and where they run near the power service.
• A communications drop keeps a vertical clearance of at least 8 ft above roofs it passes over, with limited exceptions.
• Where a power service drop of 750 volts or less runs above and parallel to a communications or coax drop, the two keep at least 12 in of separation through the span and at the building attachment.
• That separation rule holds provided the power conductors are insulated and at least 40 in of clearance is kept between the two services at the pole.
sections.on_the_job: Before you set a ladder, look up: check the comm drop's height over the roof and its distance from the power drop at the wall and back at the pole. Measure, do not eyeball — 8 ft over the roof, 12 in at the wall, 40 in at the pole. Never use the power service mast to support a communications drop. If the existing drop sags into the power drop, that is a provider call, not something to fix by pulling it tighter yourself.

sections.why_it_exists: Two drops age at different rates. A communications drop that sags onto a power drop puts line voltage on the phone and coax network, and on every piece of equipment and every hand that touches it inside. The roof clearance keeps the drop out of reach of roofers, ladders, and antennas — the people and things that move around up there — and the separation keeps a failed support from becoming a cross-contact.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer is “12 in of separation everywhere covers it.” The 12 in is only half the rule: it runs through the span and at the attachment, and it only holds while the power conductors are insulated and the pole keeps 40 in between the two services. Second trap: 8 ft is the clearance over a roof the drop passes over — not over the ground, and not a suggestion when the roof is 'barely' under the span.

sections.title: Underground cables where power is also present
sections.plain_explanation: Underground communications wires and cables that share a manhole, handhole, or similar enclosure with electric light, power, Class 1, or non-power-limited fire alarm conductors must be kept apart from those conductors by a suitable barrier. The point is simple: a space where a worker may reach in and grab a cable cannot mix exposed power conductors with communications cable as if they were the same system. The barrier has to be permanent and suitable, not a scrap of cardboard or a cable draped to the far side.
sections.why_it_exists: A handhole is dark, wet and crowded, and a worker reaching in cannot tell a communications cable from a power conductor by feel. If a jacket is nicked or a power conductor faults, the 'harmless' cable in the same space can carry line voltage to the next person who grabs it — possibly a telephone tech who never expected voltage at all. The barrier keeps two systems that share a hole from ever sharing a touch.
sections.on_the_job: Sharma rarely opens manholes, but the same thinking applies at underground entrances and pull points on light-commercial work. On a Clermont strip plaza, the crew opened a handhole to pull a camera feed and found the existing comm cable lying across the lot-lighting conductors with no barrier at all. Do not just close the lid — report it and get the separation corrected before the new cable goes in.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer is that draping the communications cable to the far side of the manhole is separation. Wrong. 800.47 wants a suitable barrier — a permanent, physical separation built into the enclosure — not distance by habit that disappears the first time someone re-dresses the cables.

sections.title: Grounding a metal conduit that carries the entrance cable
sections.plain_explanation: When the communications entrance wire or cable arrives inside a metal conduit, the conduit stops being just a sleeve. Section 800.49 requires that metal conduit to be connected, by a bonding conductor or a grounding electrode conductor, to a grounding electrode — or to the building grounding electrode system where one exists — using the connection points given in 800.100(B). First choice on that list is the intersystem bonding termination; after that come the building's grounding electrode system and the other accessible points the section names, and in a building with no grounding means at all, an electrode installed for the purpose. A floating metal entrance conduit can sit at a very different potential from the building during a surge, which is exactly what the bond prevents.
sections.on_the_job: On a Winter Garden house, the provider's entrance cable comes down the wall in a 3/4 in EMT sleeve to the demarc box. Before the provider's appointment, we set a bonding clamp on the EMT and ran the bond about 8 ft to the intersystem bonding termination at the Siemens meter-main — a listed 800.100(B) point, not the water pipe that happened to be closer. Plastic conduit would not need the bond, but it also would not extend the point of entrance the way a grounded metal raceway can, so the metal sleeve plus its bond is the better entrance.
sections.why_it_exists: The entrance conduit is a long piece of metal that starts outside the building, where lightning and utility surges arrive, and ends inside next to grounded equipment. Left floating, it can charge to a different voltage than everything around it and flash across to the nearest grounded metal — or to a person touching it. Bonding ties it to the same earth reference, so the whole entrance rises and falls together.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is landing the conduit bond on the nearest water pipe because metal is metal. Section 800.49 sends you to the connection points in 800.100(B) — the intersystem bonding termination first, then the building grounding system points the section lists. A random pipe may not be bonded to anything. Second trap: skipping the bond because the cable inside is fiber. The rule is about the metal conduit, not the signal inside it.

Conduit bond landed on a nearby water pipe or a receptacle ground instead of an 800.100(B) connection point.

sections.title: Keeping communications cable away from lightning protection
sections.plain_explanation:
Where it is practicable, communications wires and cables on a building — coax included — are kept at least 6 ft away from lightning protection system conductors.
• The 6 ft is measured between the communications cable path and the nearest lightning conductor, down leads included.
• Where 6 ft genuinely cannot be had, the separation is not guessed: it is calculated from the sideflash equation in NFPA 780, the lightning protection standard.
A down conductor carries an enormous surge for a few microseconds. A communications cable run alongside it can pick up enough of that energy by induction to destroy equipment or start a fire inside.
sections.on_the_job: Florida is lightning country, so this one is not theoretical here. On any building with air terminals and down leads — churches, schools, larger custom homes — route the data and coax entrances to a different wall or corner whenever you can. On a church job the down lead came down the east wall, so we put the coax and Cat 6 entrance on the south wall and held 9 ft between the two paths at the closest point. If the only entrance is beside a down lead, raise it with the lead before the rough-in, not at final.

sections.why_it_exists: A lightning strike does not have to hit a cable to wreck what is on it. The surge racing down a down lead throws a fast, huge magnetic pulse, and any long cable running parallel and close couples to it like the secondary of a transformer. The induced surge rides the coax or data cable straight into modems, panels and TVs. Six feet of air breaks that coupling down to a level the equipment can survive.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer is that bonding fixes it: "the comm system is bonded to the lightning protection system, so the cable can run with the down lead." Bonding ties the grounding electrodes together; it does nothing about induction along a parallel run. The 6 ft separation is still required where practicable.

sections.title: Bonding and grounding at the entrance — the heart of Chapter 8
sections.plain_explanation:
This is the section the whole chapter hangs on. It covers how communications cables and primary protectors get bonded and grounded: the metallic parts that arrive from outside — cable sheaths, protector grounds, coax shields handled under their own articles — must be tied to the building's grounding system at the entrance. The bonding or grounding conductor has its own rules, broken out on the next three pages:
• Material and size: copper or another corrosion-resistant conductive material, not smaller than 14 AWG, with capacity at least equal to the sheath or conductor it serves — and never required to be larger than 6 AWG (800.100(A)).
• Length: run as short as practicable; in a one- or two-family dwelling it may not exceed 20 ft (800.100(A)).
• Where it lands: first choice is the intersystem bonding termination; without one, the grounding electrode system or another accessible point 800.100(B) names.
• A separate communications electrode is allowed past the length limit only when it is bonded to the power grounding system with a conductor not smaller than 6 AWG (800.100(D)).
Done right, a surge arriving on a phone line or coax shield is carried to the same earth reference as the power service, so the two systems rise and fall together instead of sparking across to each other.
sections.on_the_job: Pick the protector and grounding-block location to keep this conductor as short and straight as you can. Land it at the intersystem bonding termination when one is there — that device exists precisely for this job (see 250.94, item L-060). Photograph the finished bond; it is the first thing a communications inspector looks for.
sections.sharma_note: S-09 puts the meter outside with the panel directly behind it inside, where the house allows. That same service spot is where the intersystem bonding termination belongs, so plan the communications bond to land at the service, not at a random rod driven by the cable installer.

sections.why_it_exists: Two systems with two separate earths is the failure this section prevents. Lightning or a fault can raise one ground thousands of volts above the other for a fraction of a second, and that difference appears across the television, the modem, and the person touching both. One bonded system means one reference: everything rises and falls together, and the surge leaves by the path built for it.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer is “drive a separate rod for the cable system and keep it away from the power ground — cleaner that way.” Backwards. A separate communications electrode must be bonded to the power grounding electrode system with 6 AWG or larger (800.100(D)); two unbonded earths are the hazard, not the cure. Second trap: sizing the bond off the service size. The floor is 14 AWG, and it never has to be larger than 6 AWG.

sections.title: The bonding conductor itself — material, size, and length
sections.plain_explanation:
The conductor that bonds the protector or cable sheath has to be copper or another corrosion-resistant conductive material, solid or stranded, and listed for the purpose, with the insulation choices the section allows.
• Not smaller than 14 AWG
• Its ampacity at least that of the metallic sheath or protected conductor it serves — but it never has to be larger than 6 AWG
• Run as short as practicable, and in a one- or two-family dwelling not over 20 ft
• Where it runs in a metal raceway, that raceway is bonded at both ends
• Run in as straight a line as practicable, and protected from physical damage
sections.on_the_job: On a Winter Garden slab home, the coax and phone protectors land on the garage wall and the intersystem bonding termination sits beside the Siemens meter-main, 11 ft away. A 14 AWG copper bonding conductor run straight along the wall lands at 11 ft — inside the 20 ft dwelling limit with room to spare. At a second house the only legal landing point measured 24 ft from the protector, so the protector moved to the other side of the meter instead of stretching the conductor past the limit. Measure the run before you mount the protector, not after.
sections.why_it_exists: This conductor is the path a lightning surge or a power-contact fault takes off the cable sheath and the protector. A thin, long, or wandering conductor has impedance exactly when the surge needs a low-impedance path, so the surge looks for another route — through equipment, or through a person. Short, straight, and adequately sized keeps the surge on the conductor and off everything else. That is why this section cares about the conductor itself — its material, its size, and its length — and not only about where it lands.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is reading 6 AWG as the minimum size. Six AWG is the ceiling — the conductor never has to be larger than 6 AWG, however big the sheath. The floor is 14 AWG, and between the two the conductor's ampacity must at least match the metallic sheath or protected conductor it serves.

sections.title: Where the bonding conductor is allowed to land
sections.plain_explanation:
This part lists, in order, the places the entrance bonding or grounding conductor may terminate.
• First choice is the intersystem bonding termination, if the building has one.
• Without one, it lands on the building's grounding electrode system or one of the accessible grounding points the section names, such as the grounding electrode conductor or the service equipment enclosure, following the exact list in the printed section.
• In a building with no grounding means at all, it lands on an electrode installed for the purpose — a rod at least 5 ft long and 1/2 in in diameter is the minimum the section describes for that case.
sections.on_the_job: New townhouse in Winter Garden: the Siemens meter-main has an intersystem bonding termination, so the cable and phone bonds land there — first choice, done. On an older Orlando ranch with no IBT, land on the grounding electrode conductor at the service, the nearest accessible point on the list. Use the first landing point on the list that the building actually has, and use the nearest accessible one. Do not land the bond on a random receptacle ground, a plumbing vent, or a rod you cannot prove is bonded to the power system. Item L-060 (250.94) explains the termination device itself.

sections.why_it_exists: Every communications entrance has to end up at the same electrical reference as the power system. If the cable plant bonds to one point and the power system to another, lightning or a fault puts the difference between those points across the equipment — and across anyone touching both. The ordered list exists so the installer takes the best available landing instead of inventing one.

New rod driven at the cable entrance while the building's grounding electrode system sits unused.
Purpose-installed rod shorter than 5 ft or under 1/2 in diameter.
Bond landed on a rod with no proof it is bonded to the power grounding electrode system.
IBT present at the meter-main but the bond run past it to a farther point.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is driving a fresh rod wherever the cable enters and calling it grounded. A rod installed for the purpose is the last landing on the list, for a building with no grounding means at all — and at minimum 5 ft long and 1/2 in in diameter. If the building has a grounding electrode system, the bond belongs on the list, not on a new rod of your own.

sections.title: Bonding a separate communications electrode back to the power system
sections.plain_explanation:
Sometimes the bonding conductor for a communications entrance cannot stay inside its length limit — in a dwelling, 800.100(A) caps that run at 20 ft. When it cannot, a separate ground rod may be driven for the communications system at the entrance. Section 800.100(D) then adds the condition that makes that separate electrode safe:
• The separate electrode is never allowed to stand alone
• It must be bonded to the building's power grounding electrode system
• The bonding conductor is no smaller than 6 AWG
Two unbonded earth connections at one house are worse than one, because a surge can put thousands of volts between them — right across the equipment inside the house.
sections.on_the_job: Orlando two-story: the meter-main is on the west wall and the cable and phone demarc is on the east wall, about 34 ft of bonding-conductor route away — past the 20 ft dwelling limit. We drive a rod at the demarc, land the protector bond on it, and then run a 6 AWG copper bond from that rod back to the power grounding electrode system at the meter-main. The same 6 AWG bonding rule shows up again for antennas in 810.21(J) and for CATV in 820.100(D) — learn it once, use it three times.
sections.why_it_exists: Earth is not at one uniform voltage during a lightning strike or a utility surge. Two separate rods can sit at very different potentials for the instant that matters, and the difference shows up between the coax shield and the power ground inside a TV or a modem. The 6 AWG bond forces both systems to rise and fall together, so that difference never appears across the equipment.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer is 'the separate rod is the communications ground, so the job is done.' A separate electrode standing by itself is exactly what 800.100(D) forbids: the rod is permitted only with the 6 AWG bond back to the power system. The second trap is the size: 14 AWG is the floor for the protector bonding conductor in 800.100(A), but the electrode-to-system bond in (D) is 6 AWG minimum.

sections.title: Grounding the primary protector at a mobile home
sections.plain_explanation:
A mobile home gets its own version of the 800.100 protector-grounding recipe, because the power service usually is not on the home itself. Under 550.32(A) the service equipment or disconnecting means sits nearby — in sight from the home and not more than 30 ft from its exterior wall.
• Where that equipment is in place, the primary protector is grounded and bonded into that grounding arrangement, as 800.100 describes.
• Where there is no mobile home service equipment or grounded disconnect in sight and within 30 ft, 800.106(A) sends the grounding to the electrode options in 800.100(B)(3) — the same list used at a building with no intersystem bonding termination and no grounding means.
• Either way, 800.106(B) adds a step an ordinary house does not need: bond the protector's grounding terminal to the mobile home's metal frame, or to the grounding terminal the home provides, with copper not smaller than 12 AWG.
This section is also why the 6 AWG bond-back rule in 800.100(D) carries a mobile-home exception — at a mobile home, 800.106 replaces it.
sections.on_the_job: Manufactured home in a Florida park: find the pedestal first. It stands 18 ft from the home's exterior wall, in plain sight, so the protector grounds into the pedestal's grounding system — and the crew still adds the 12 AWG copper bond from the protector's grounding terminal to the home's frame rail. On the next call the pedestal is 45 ft away: that job is on the 800.100(B)(3) electrode list, and the frame bond is still required. A rod by itself never replaces it.
sections.figure_idea: A mobile home with its power pedestal nearby: the protector at the entrance grounded into the pedestal system, with the 12 AWG bond drawn from the protector to the home's frame; beside it, the same home with the pedestal far away and a local electrode driven at the home.

sections.why_it_exists: A mobile home sits on piers, and its metal frame is the biggest thing the occupants touch. If the telephone protector grounds to one electrode and the frame sits at another potential, a surge puts that difference across the phone, the appliances and the people between them. The 12 AWG frame bond forces the protector ground and the frame to rise and fall together.
inspection_fails: No bond between the protector grounding terminal and the mobile home frame — the write-up on almost every manufactured-home call.
Frame bond smaller than 12 AWG, or run in aluminum — 800.106(B) calls for copper.
Protector grounded to a lone rod beside the home while a grounded pedestal sits 20 ft away in plain sight.
Protector grounded into the pedestal system when the disconnect is 45 ft from the wall — wrong case; the 800.100(B)(3) electrode list applies.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is "the protector has its own ground rod, so it is grounded." A lone rod does not tie the telephone ground to the frame the occupants touch, and it does not satisfy 800.106. The frame bond — copper, 12 AWG minimum — is required in every case, whichever grounding route the protector takes.

sections.title: Raceways and cable routing assemblies for communications
sections.plain_explanation: Communications wires and cables may be run in communications raceways and cable routing assemblies, as long as both are listed and chosen for the space they serve — plenum, riser, or general-purpose — under the application tables in 800.154. The raceway levels track the cable levels in 800.179 and the listing rules in 800.182, and a point from 800.182 is worth memorizing here: a rated raceway does not upgrade the cable inside it, so a plenum raceway in an air-handling space still has to contain plenum-rated CMP cable. Chapter 9 conduit-fill rules do not govern ordinary communications cables in these raceways. The section keeps one exception: medium-power network-powered broadband cables. In other words, a listed low-voltage raceway is its own wiring method here; do not borrow a Chapter 3 conduit rule and assume it decides the question.
sections.on_the_job: On a light-commercial job in Kissimmee — a small medical office — the data runs cross an air-handling ceiling, so the spec is plenum-level raceway with CMP cable inside; the run down the shaft to the first floor is riser level with CMR. We kept the manufacturer's fill guidance for the cable routing assembly even though Chapter 9 fill percentages are not the governing rule — the listing still expects the cable supported and not crushed. And one boundary to respect: if the job is really Class 2 or Class 3 control wiring, you are in Article 725 (Chapter 7), not here.
sections.why_it_exists: The raceway levels exist because of fire and smoke, not electricity. A pathway that runs through an air-handling ceiling or a vertical shaft is a ready-made route for smoke to travel between spaces, so the pathway and the cable in it are both rated for the space. The fill exception exists for the opposite reason: a medium-power broadband cable carries real power alongside the signal, so it is treated more like a power cable than a whisper of data.
sections.exam_trap: Two traps meet on this page. First: the raceway is plenum-rated, so the CM cable inside it is fine in the plenum. No — 800.182 is explicit that the raceway does not upgrade the cable; each is matched to the space on its own. Second: applying Chapter 9 conduit-fill percentages to a listed communications raceway. Chapter 9 fill does not govern ordinary communications cables here — the only exception the section keeps is medium-power network-powered broadband cable.

CM cable pulled through a plenum raceway in a plenum space — the raceway's rating does not upgrade the cable (800.182).
Unlisted channel or hardware-store PVC used as a raceway for communications cable — 800.110 requires listed raceways and cable routing assemblies.
Cable routing assembly stuffed past the manufacturer's fill guidance and left unsupported between floors.

sections.title: Installing cables inside the building — ducts, plenums, and risers
sections.plain_explanation:
This long section is the inside-the-building installation rulebook for communications cable.
• Cables in ducts made for environmental air follow the duct rules the section references.
• Cables in other air-handling spaces (plenums) must be the plenum types allowed there — CMP.
• Vertical runs that pass through one or more floors — risers — need riser-rated cable (CMR), or one of the protected alternatives the section lists, such as cable in a metal raceway or a fireproof shaft with firestops at each floor.
• One- and two-family dwellings get their own, more relaxed list, which is why house work and commercial work part company here.
• Cables installed inside must be listed, and a voltage rating is not to be marked on a communications cable, because that marking invites someone to treat it as power wire.
sections.on_the_job: Before rough-in, ask one question per run: is this space moving air, or does this run pass a floor? A yes to the first means CMP; a yes to the second means CMR or a listed protected path. On a two-story Winter Park office, the Cat 6A home runs cross a return-air ceiling plenum and then drop down a shaft to the first-floor rack — one cable has to satisfy both spaces, so CMP goes in everywhere on that job. At a house, CM or CMX from the dwelling list is normally the right shelf to shop from.
sections.figure_idea: A three-panel figure: a plenum ceiling space labelled CMP, a vertical shaft between floors labelled CMR, and a same-floor office run labelled CM/CMG.
sections.why_it_exists: In a fire, cable jackets are fuel and smoke spreaders. A plenum is part of the air system, so a burning ordinary cable pumps smoke into every room the air handler serves. A riser shaft is a chimney between floors. Matching the cable's fire rating to the space keeps the cable from becoming the path the fire and smoke take through the building.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is shopping by category instead of by fire rating: a Cat 6 cable is not automatically legal in a plenum or a riser. The letters CMP, CMR, CMG, CM and CMX rate fire behavior, not speed. A second trap: a voltage rating printed on the jacket — the section forbids marking one on communications cable, because it invites someone to treat the cable as power wire.

sections.title: Separation from power — the section in one view
sections.plain_explanation:
Communications cables must be kept apart from electric light, power, Class 1, and non-power-limited fire alarm conductors. This page is the whole section in one view; the next two pages take the halves one at a time.
• Sharing: comm cable may not sit in the same raceway, box, or enclosure with power conductors unless a separation setup covered on the next page genuinely applies (800.133(A)(1)).
• Open runs: where comm cable runs alongside power wiring in the open, keep at least 2 in between them (800.133(A)(2)).
• Support: never use the outside of a raceway as a support for communications cable (800.133(B)).
sections.on_the_job: Keep low-voltage cable out of power boxes and power raceways unless a listed barrier setup on the next page genuinely applies. Do not strap, tape, or tie a data or coax run to the outside of a conduit for support. The classic Florida spec-house fail is the shared stud bay: Cat 6 zip-tied to a branch-circuit home run down the same stud. Split them — their own holes, 2 in apart in the open. When an inspector says 'separation,' this section is what they mean, and the distance is 2 in, confirmed against the 2020 text, not the larger figures in some exam-prep sheets.

sections.why_it_exists: Power conductors are the energy source in the wall. A comm cable lashed against them picks up induced voltage on a good day. On a bad day — a fault, a surge, a nail through both cables — full line voltage lands on phone and data jacks all over the house, on equipment and people never built for it. Separation is what keeps the low-voltage system low-voltage.

sections.exam_trap: The trap answer is 12 in — or 'they can never be in the same building.' In the open, the number is 2 in. The reverse trap catches just as many: because 2 in works in the open, apprentices assume a shared box is fine with a little space inside it. It is not. Sharing a raceway or box is the (A)(1) half of the rule, with its own barrier conditions.

sections.title: Sharing a raceway, box, or enclosure with power
sections.plain_explanation:
Communications conductors are not permitted in the same raceway, box, or enclosure as electric light, power, Class 1, or non-power-limited fire alarm conductors as a general rule. The exceptions are narrow:
• Sharing is allowed where the two systems are separated by a permanent barrier or a listed divider.
• Power conductors may be brought into a communications enclosure only to feed the communications equipment itself, routed inside the enclosure to keep at least 1/4 in (6 mm) of separation from the communications wiring (800.133(A)(1), Exception No. 2).
A shared box with a listed divider is a designed product, not two cables stuffed into one handy box.
sections.on_the_job: Structured-wiring panel in a Lake Nona home: the panel needs a receptacle inside it to power the switch and modem. That power feed may enter the communications enclosure because it feeds the communications equipment itself — and inside, we route it dressed away from the Cat 6 bundle, keeping at least 1/4 in (6 mm) of separation. sections.title: The 2-inch separation in open runs
sections.plain_explanation:
Where communications conductors run near power or Class 1 conductors outside a shared enclosure, they must be separated by at least 2 in. That 2 in can be provided by space alone, or by one of the constructions the section recognizes:
• Power conductors in a raceway, or in a metal-sheathed, armored, nonmetallic-sheathed, or UF cable assembly — the sheath or raceway already provides the separation
• The communications cable in its own raceway
What the rule will not accept is communications cable laid directly against open power wiring with nothing between them.
sections.on_the_job: Sharma practice is stricter than the code here: in a stud bay, drill separate holes and keep the 2 in, and in an attic do not lay Cat 6 across a bundle of Romex and call the joist a separator. The Code itself is satisfied where the power conductors are in a raceway or a sheathed cable assembly (the NM sheath counts) — the house habit keeps the 2 in anyway. If a crossing is unavoidable, cross at right angles rather than running parallel in contact, and keep the parallel distance honest everywhere else.
sections.figure_idea: A stud-bay drawing with two bored holes 2 in apart, one holding NM cable and one holding Cat 6, plus an inset showing NM's sheath counting as the separation where the rule allows it.
sections.why_it_exists: Communications cable is built for signals, not for line voltage. Run tight against power wiring, it picks up induced voltage and hum, and a fault — or a nail through both cables — can put 120 V on a phone line, a network jack, or the technician holding it. Two inches of space, or a sheath or raceway doing the same job, keeps the two systems out of each other's failures.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is demanding 2 in of empty air everywhere. Where the power conductors are in a raceway or a sheathed cable assembly — NM counts — or the communications cable is in its own raceway, the bare 2 in is not demanded, because the construction already provides the separation. The opposite trap also fails: inside a shared box, the rule is (A)(1)'s barrier or divider, not this 2 in. And a joist between the two cables is not a construction the section recognizes — the separation is measured between the cables themselves.

sections.title: Where each cable type may be used — the application tables
sections.plain_explanation:
The tables in this section are the permission slip for cable types: they match listed communications cables against the places each type may be installed — plenums, risers, general use, dwellings. A higher-rated cable may substitute for a lower one down the ladder; a lower-rated cable may never substitute upward.
• CMP — plenum spaces, and anywhere a lower type may run
• CMR — risers and general use; not plenums
• CMG and CM — general use and dwellings; not plenums or risers (one shared rung — either may stand in for the other)
• CMX — limited use in dwellings, and in raceways and short exposed runs within the conditions the table sets
The ladder order and the substitutions are the same ones stated on the cable-types page (800.179).
sections.on_the_job: When a supplier substitutes cable, check the jacket legend against the space, not against the purchase order. On a Lake Nona medical office rough-in, the delivered Cat 6A was CM where the ceiling was a return-air plenum; the CMP on the order was the right cable and the CM went back, because CMP can go almost anywhere communications cable can go and CM cannot go in that ceiling. CMX cannot leave its dwelling lane at all.
sections.unverified_reason: Still unverified after Mike Holt recheck (2026-11-25): The ladder content is correct (CMP > CMR > CMG/CM > CMX; no upward substitution). But the 2020 edition restructured Chapter 8: Article 800 became the general article and communications circuits moved to Article 805. I could not confirm first-hand whether the 2020 Table 800.154(a) also carries the CATV (coax) types, which would make the page's statement that coax "has its own application table, Table 820.154" a 2017 holdover. Check the 2020 table titles and contents, then fix the cross-reference. Also add that CMX is limited to dwellings, raceways and short exposed runs per the table conditions.
sections.why_it_exists: The ladder exists because fire behaves differently in each space. A plenum moves air — and smoke — to every room it serves. A riser shaft is a chimney between floors. A cable rated for a harsher space can serve a milder one, but the reverse puts a cable that burns and smokes too freely into the space where that does the most harm. Downward substitution is safe; upward substitution hands smoke a distribution system. The tables in this section are where the ladder becomes the rule for each space: they say, space by space, which types may run there.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is substituting upward to finish the job: CM in a plenum or CMX in a riser 'because it was on the truck.' Substitution runs one way only — down the ladder. The mirror trap is wasting CMP money everywhere out of habit; the table lets each space take its own type, and dwellings have the widest list.

sections.title: The cable types themselves — CMP, CMR, CMG, CM, CMX
sections.plain_explanation:
This section defines the listed communications cable types by how they behave in fire. Type CMP is the plenum type, tested for low flame spread and smoke in air-handling spaces. Type CMR is the riser type, for vertical runs between floors, and Types CMG and CM are general-purpose types for ordinary horizontal runs. Type CMX is the limited-use type, restricted in size and use, and at home mainly in one- and two-family dwellings. Conductors in these cables are copper, other than in coaxial constructions handled under Article 820. The letters say nothing about speed or category — a CMP Cat 5e and a CM Cat 6 are rated by fire behavior, not performance.
Substitutions run downhill only (800.154):
• CMP may stand in for any type below it.
• CMR may stand in for CMG, CM or CMX.
• CMG may stand in for CM or CMX, and CM may stand in for CMX.
• Nothing substitutes upward — CMX never replaces CM, and CM never goes in a riser or a plenum.
sections.on_the_job: Read the jacket before you pull: the type letters decide where the cable may go, and the category marking decides what it can carry. Do not let a cheap roll of CMX talk you into a commercial riser. Keep one shelf rule in your head: plenum space, CMP; between floors, CMR; same floor, CM or CMG; house, CM or CMX within its limits.

sections.why_it_exists: In a fire, cable is a fuse that runs through the whole building. The wrong jacket carries flame from floor to floor through a riser, and cable burning in an air-handling space puts smoke straight into the breathing air of every room the system serves. The type ladder exists so the cable in each space has been tested for exactly the way fire and smoke behave in that space.

A CM cable in a plenum fails no matter what it can carry. Second trap: reading CMX as a general commercial type. It is limited-use, and at home mainly in one- and two-family dwellings.

sections.title: Grounding hardware has to be listed
sections.plain_explanation:
Where bonding or grounding is required, the devices used to connect a shield, sheath, or other non-current-carrying metallic member of a cable to a bonding conductor or a grounding electrode conductor must be listed — or be part of listed equipment.
• 800.100 specifies the conductor itself — its material, its size, its length, and where it may land. This section governs the clamp or fitting that joins the cable's metal to that conductor.
• A primary protector or network interface device with its own grounding terminal satisfies the rule through its listing.
• A random piece of hardware does not. If the fitting is not listed for grounding and bonding, it does not count, however solid it looks.
sections.on_the_job: Use the grounding terminal built into the protector or interface device, or a listed grounding clamp made for bonding a cable shield or sheath. At a house entrance that is the listed clamp on the grounding block, landed with the 14 AWG bond from 800.100. A hose clamp, a sheet-metal screw driven through the sheath, or an unmarked clamp off the hardware shelf is not a listed grounding device — and the fitting at the entrance is exactly where a sharp inspector looks first.

sections.why_it_exists: The clamp is the weak link in every entrance bond. An unlisted fitting corrodes, works loose, or bites through the shield it was supposed to protect, and the bond silently opens — the conductor still hangs there looking grounded while surge energy has no path out. Listed hardware is tested to clamp the cable it is made for, stay tight, and carry the current the bond exists to carry.

sections.title: Communications raceways and cable routing assemblies — the listing rules
sections.plain_explanation:
This section is the listing home for the two support systems Article 800 builds communications installations with:
• Communications raceways — the enclosed nonmetallic channels defined in Article 100, close cousins of ENT.
• Cable routing assemblies — the single or multiple channels that support high densities of cable.
The raceway rules follow the same three fire levels as the cables themselves — plenum, riser, and general-purpose — and the section carries two marking tables, Table 800.182(a) for cable routing assemblies and Table 800.182(b) for communications raceways, so the level is printed on the product.
One point installers miss: a rated raceway does not upgrade the cable inside it. A plenum communications raceway in an air-handling space under 300.22(C) still has to contain plenum-rated CMP cable. The raceway and the cable are each matched to the space on their own.
sections.on_the_job: Office fit-out in Orlando with a return-air ceiling plenum. The print on the raceway has to read plenum level before it is hung, and the cable pulled into it is CMP — both, not one of two. The run down the shaft gets riser-level raceway and CMR cable; the ordinary office runs get general-purpose. Nonmetallic communications raceways go in under the ENT rules this section points to — bends, supports, and joints per 362.24 through 362.56 — and cable routing assemblies support their cable at the intervals the listing allows.

Matching the raceway's fire level to the space keeps the support system from spreading flame and smoke — and the cable inside needs its own matching rating, because the raceway is not a fireproof box.

sections.title: Article 805 — Communications circuits
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 805 is where the old pre-2020 Article 800 went to live. It covers the traditional communications circuits — the telephone-style circuits that run from the service provider's demarcation point to the customer's communications equipment — and the specific rules for those circuits that Article 800 does not already state generally. Its working topics:
• Which circuits need a primary protector, and where it goes (805.90)
• How the metallic sheath of an entering cable is grounded or interrupted at the entrance (805.93)
• The one communications outlet every new dwelling unit owes (805.156)
If Article 800 is the chapter's foundation, Article 805 is the phone-and-data entrance built on it.
sections.on_the_job: Most of Sharma's houses touch this article lightly: a demarc, a protector, a bond, and one outlet. On a new house in Sanford the whole 805 job is the demarc box on the garage wall, the provider's primary protector bonded under 800.100 with a run of about 6 ft to the intersystem bonding termination, the entering cable's sheath bonded at that same point, and one communications outlet roughed in and cabled back to the demarc. The failures are just as light — no protector where one is required, a sheath left floating, no outlet roughed in. Catch them at rough-in, when they are still cheap.

NEC 2023 applies in Florida only to permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026 (FBC 9th Ed.), so until then a 2023 study book may show different Chapter 8 numbering or wording.

sections.why_it_exists: A communications circuit is a wire that starts miles away, on poles and in plant the building owner does not control, and ends at a phone or a modem inside. Lightning and accidental contact with power conductors ride that wire indoors. Article 805 is the entrance discipline that stops the energy at the door: a protector to shunt it, a sheath grounded or interrupted so it cannot carry a surge deep into the building, and a bond that ties it all to the same earth as the power service.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is citing 800.156 for the dwelling-unit outlet. That was the pre-2020 address; the 2020 reorganization moved the rule to 805.156, and older checklists and study guides still carry the old number. Second trap: treating Article 800 as the whole story for a phone circuit. Article 800 states the general rules; the circuit-specific duties — protectors, sheath, the outlet — live in 805.

sections.title: Scope of communications circuits
sections.plain_explanation:
This short section fixes what Article 805 covers: communications circuits and the equipment on them. A communications circuit, as the chapter defines it, is the path that extends service from the communications utility or service provider up to and including the customer's own communications equipment.
• Phone and provider data circuits and their entrance equipment: Article 805, with the general rules of Article 800.
• Inside wiring that is really power-limited control or signaling work: Article 725 in Chapter 7 instead.
The same physical cable can fall under different articles depending on what system it serves, so the system, not the jacket color, decides.
sections.on_the_job: When a low-voltage scope is handed to you, ask what system each run serves before you pick an article. Phone and provider data entrance: 805 and 800. Door access, HVAC controls, and most security signaling: usually 725. On a Florida small-commercial fit-out, the same spool of Cat 6 can feed a provider phone jack in the morning (805) and a thermostat after lunch (725) — the paperwork, separation, and inspection standard change with the system, not the spool. Guessing the article is how separation and listing rules get crossed.

sections.title: Circuits that require primary protectors — and the 4-inch rule outside
sections.plain_explanation:
805.50 works with 805.90: it identifies the communications circuits that require primary protectors and sets the conditions on the wiring that feeds them.
• Part (A): the drop and entrance conductors used to extend circuits to a building must be listed for the purpose.
• Part (B): specified unshielded communications wires and cables installed on the outside of a building must be separated at least 4 in from open electric light or power wiring that is not in a raceway or a cable assembly — subject to the alternatives and exceptions the section allows.
• Part (C): circuits entering the building ahead of the primary protector must be protected by a bushing or a metal raceway, unless an exception applies — entry through masonry, or a listed fuseless-protector arrangement, for example.
sections.on_the_job: Rear wall of a small office in Ocala: the telephone drop comes down the wall about 2 in from open power wiring carried on insulators. That fails part (B) — rework the drop so the separation is 4 in or more, or use one of the alternatives the section allows. Do not reach for the indoor number here: the 2 in separation of 800.133(A)(2) is an inside rule, and the two numbers are not interchangeable. At the entrance, the circuit comes in ahead of the primary protector through a metal raceway — not through a plain hole drilled in the wood framing.

sections.why_it_exists: The outside run is the exposed run. A communications drop sitting against open power wiring picks up fault voltage and surge energy before the protector ever sees it, and conductors that enter ahead of the protector unprotected carry that energy straight past the device meant to stop it. The 4 in of air and the protected entry keep the primary protector as the first thing a surge meets.

The indoor 2 in separation cited to justify an outside run that requires 4 in.

On the outside of the building, 805.50(B) requires 4 in from open light or power wiring that is not in a raceway or cable assembly. The reverse trap also appears — demanding 4 in between cables sharing an indoor box, where 800.133(A) governs.

sections.title: Primary protectors — where they are required and where they go
sections.plain_explanation:
A listed primary protector is required on each communications circuit that is exposed to lightning, or exposed to accidental contact with power conductors operating at over 300 volts to ground. The protector is an arrester connected between each line conductor and ground, mounted the way its listing directs, with its terminals marked for line and ground.
• It sits in, on, or immediately next to the building it serves, as close as practicable to the point where the circuit enters.
• It never goes in a hazardous (classified) location, or near easily ignitible material.
• The section recognizes fused and fuseless designs; a fuseless protector is permitted only where the conditions the section lists are met.
• Secondary protectors may be added inside, in series between the primary protector and the equipment it serves.
sections.on_the_job: Aerial phone and coax drops come into a Winter Garden house on the same wall as the Siemens meter-main. Mount the listed primary protector in its enclosure right at the entrance, beside the service, and bond it under 800.100 with the shortest honest run to the intersystem bonding termination — short protector ground, short trouble. If a circuit arrives exposed with no protector, that is a stop-and-call item for the provider or the lead, not a detail to wave through at trim.

sections.why_it_exists: An outside drop is a long conductor hanging in the weather. It collects lightning energy and, if a support fails, it can land on a power conductor. Without an arrester at the entrance, that energy rides the pair straight to the phone system, the network gear, and anyone touching it. The protector gives the surge a short, deliberate path to ground at the door instead of through the building.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer is “the protector can go anywhere inside, as long as it is ahead of the equipment.” Location is part of the rule: in, on, or immediately next to the building, as close as practicable to the entrance, and never in a classified location. Second trap: picking a fuseless protector because it is cheaper. Fuseless is permitted only under the conditions 805.90 lists, not as a free choice.

sections.title: Grounding or interrupting the cable sheath at the entrance
sections.plain_explanation: The non-current-carrying metallic sheath members of a communications cable entering a building must be dealt with at the entrance: either grounded following 800.100, or interrupted by an insulating joint or an equivalent device, as near as practicable to the point where the cable enters. A floating metallic sheath is a long antenna that delivers surge energy deep into the building. Grounding it at the entrance, or breaking its continuity there with an insulating joint, keeps that energy outside the living space. Section 805.93 gives exactly those two choices — there is no third option of leaving the sheath floating.
sections.on_the_job: At the demarc of an Orlando duplex rewire, the entering communications cable's shield disappears into the wall unbonded and there is no insulating joint — flag it before anything gets closed up. The fix at the entrance: bond the sheath per 800.100 with a 14 AWG minimum conductor to the intersystem bonding termination, or fit an insulating joint at the entry point. This is the communications twin of the coax rule in 820.93 — same entrance, same idea.

sections.why_it_exists: The sheath is bonded to the outside plant, so it arrives at the wall carrying whatever the outside world put on it — lightning energy, fault voltage, induced surges. If that metal runs unbroken and ungrounded into the building, the energy goes looking for a path through equipment and people indoors. Dealing with the sheath at the entrance keeps the energy at the wall, where it belongs.

Insulating joint installed mid-run, leaving the entrance section of sheath unbroken and ungrounded.
Bonding conductor landed on an unlisted point instead of following 800.100.
sections.exam_trap: The sheath can be grounded anywhere convenient inside the building — say, at the far-end equipment rack. Wrong. 805.93 puts the treatment as near as practicable to the point of entry. Ground it deep inside and the surge energy still travels the full length of the building to get there.

sections.title: One communications outlet in every new dwelling
sections.plain_explanation:
For new construction, every dwelling unit gets at least one communications outlet. Three conditions ride on it:
• The outlet is installed inside the dwelling, in a readily accessible area
• It is cabled back to the service provider demarcation point
• It is roughed in whether or not a provider has been chosen yet
This is the rule that used to live at 800.156 before the 2020 reorganization moved it to 805.156, which is why older checklists and study guides still cite the old number. One outlet is the floor, not a design. Sharma's builders routinely want data and coax in several rooms, but the Code's own minimum is this single, cabled, accessible outlet.
sections.on_the_job: New slab home in Kissimmee: the demarc lands on the garage wall where the provider drops arrive. From there we run one Cat 6 home run — about 55 ft — to a communications outlet on the living room wall, on an open stretch the owner can reach without moving furniture. The builder's plan adds coax and data to the bedrooms and the office, and we rough those in too, but if the plan had shown nothing, the one living room outlet is what the inspector is looking for. Rough it in even when the buyer has not picked a provider — a cabled outlet at the demarc is the requirement, not a live dial tone. And when an old Sharma checklist says 800.156, translate it: in the 2020 book it is 805.156.
sections.why_it_exists: A dwelling with no cabled communications outlet is a house the phone and internet installers have to retrofit later — surface wiring, drilled floors, or a wireless-only service the owner never chose. The rule treats one outlet as basic infrastructure that has to be roughed in while the walls are open, because adding it after the drywall costs far more and usually looks it.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is the old number and the wrong count. An answer citing 800.156 is citing the pre-2020 book — in the 2020 edition the rule is 805.156. The other wrong answer is 'one outlet per room': the Code minimum is one outlet per dwelling unit. Extra outlets are a builder spec, not a Code count.

sections.title: Article 810 — Radio and television equipment
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 810 covers antenna systems:
• Receiving antennas for radio and television, and satellite dishes
• Their masts and lead-in conductors
• Amateur and citizen-band transmitting and receiving stations
Uniquely in this chapter, Article 810 is not covered by the general rules of Article 800 — it stands alone, and its own grounding section, 810.21, is the complete recipe for bonding an antenna system: the mast, the discharge unit and the run to ground are all answered inside the article. Its concerns are the ones Florida weather writes large: lightning, wind-blown lead-ins, and keeping antenna wiring clear of power conductors.
sections.on_the_job: A dish or antenna job is a grounding job with a picture at the end of it. Price and plan the mast bond, the discharge unit, and the run to a legal grounding point before anyone climbs: the bonding conductor is 10 AWG copper minimum under 810.21(H), and if a separate rod gets driven for the antenna, it bonds back to the power grounding system with 6 AWG under 810.21(J) — it never stands alone. If a mast stands within 5 ft of a swimming pool, it also has to bond to the pool's equipotential grid — see the pool rules in Chapter 6.
sections.florida_note: Florida's lightning exposure makes 810.21 the most safety-critical page in this article here. Local amendments and insurer requirements on existing lightning protection systems vary; confirm with the AHJ on larger homes.
sections.why_it_exists: An antenna is usually the tallest metal on the house, wired straight into the most sensitive electronics in it. A strike on or near the mast — or a lead-in blown across a power conductor in a storm — puts that energy on the coax and into the building. Article 810's grounding recipe gives the energy a deliberate path to earth that does not run through the television, the receiver, or the person touching them.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is reaching for Article 800 on an antenna job. Article 810 stands alone: the bonding sizes and the whole grounding recipe are in 810.21, not in 800.100. The second trap is treating the antenna's own ground rod as the finished job — a separate electrode still needs its 6 AWG bond back to the power system.

sections.title: Grounding the mast and its supporting structure
sections.plain_explanation:
Outdoor antenna masts, and the metal structures that support antennas, must be grounded following 810.21.
• The mast bonding or grounding conductor is sized by 810.21 — not smaller than 10 AWG copper (810.21(H)).
• There is one narrow escape: an antenna and its supporting mast or structure that sit inside a zone of protection — the area sheltered by a lightning protection system, described with a 150 ft radius rolling sphere in the lightning standard — are not required to be grounded under this section.
Outside that protected zone, which means nearly every ordinary house dish and mast Sharma will meet, the mast gets its 810.21 bond, full stop.
sections.on_the_job: Do not let “the dish is small” talk you out of the mast bond. Look for a nearby lightning protection system before claiming the zone-of-protection exception — on a normal subdivision house in Florida there is none, so ground the mast. Keep the bond run straight and protected, per 810.21, and land it on the building grounding system where 810.21 points.

sections.why_it_exists: A mast is usually the highest metal on the house, holding a conductor that runs straight inside to the TV or receiver. Lightning does not have to hit it directly — a nearby strike can drive surge energy down the lead-in. The 810.21 bond gives that energy a controlled path to earth at the mast instead of through the equipment and the house wiring.

sections.title: Clearances for antenna lead-in conductors
sections.plain_explanation:
Lead-in conductors from an outdoor antenna have clearance rules in three directions:
• On the building: keep the lead-in from swinging closer than 2 ft to conductors of circuits of 250 volts or less, and at least 10 ft from conductors of circuits over 250 volts.
• From lightning protection: at least 6 ft from lightning protection conductors.
• Underground and indoors: underground lead-ins keep at least 12 in from power conductors, and indoor antenna and lead-in conductors keep at least 2 in from light and power conductors.
The conductors themselves are sized from the table in 810.16 by material and length — a lead-in under 35 ft can be as small as 19 AWG copper, while runs over 150 ft step up to 12 AWG copper, with copper-clad steel and bronze sizes listed alongside.
sections.on_the_job: Route the lead-in like it will move in wind, because in a Florida storm it will: the clearance is to the swung position, not the calm-day position. On a house with a roof mast, check the swing against the 120/240 service drop before the mast height is final — that drop is a circuit of 250 volts or less, so the number is 2 ft. Keep the indoor tail 2 in off power wiring, the same number as 800.133(A)(2). Long spans need the bigger wire from the 810.16 table, not whatever is on the truck.

sections.why_it_exists: A lead-in is a long wire on a mast, swinging in the wind, wired straight into the house. If it swings into a power conductor — or a power conductor falls across it — line voltage rides the antenna wire indoors to the equipment and to whoever touches it. The clearances are written to the swung position, not the calm-day position, and the 6 ft from lightning conductors keeps a strike's sideflash from jumping onto the antenna system.

sections.title: Antenna discharge units
sections.plain_explanation:
Each lead-in conductor from an outdoor antenna gets its own listed antenna discharge unit, or an equivalent means the section allows. The unit's job is to drain static charges off the antenna system before they reach the equipment inside. Placement has three parts:
• As near as practicable to the point where the lead-in enters the building — inside or outside the wall
• Not near combustible material
• Not in a hazardous (classified) location
A discharge unit with nowhere to drain is decoration: the unit itself must be bonded or grounded following 810.21, which is what gives the drained charge somewhere to go.
sections.on_the_job: A Lake Mary house has two lead-ins: a roof antenna for local channels and the dish. That means two discharge units, mounted on the outside wall right where the lead-ins enter, each bonded with 10 AWG copper down to the intersystem bonding termination — about a 9 ft run, straight. The dish lead-in came with a factory grounding block; we checked its listing before counting it as the discharge unit instead of assuming the block was listed for that duty. One unit per lead-in, at the entrance, bonded per 810.21 — that is the whole checklist.
sections.why_it_exists: An antenna and its lead-in are a collector: wind-driven rain and dust build static charge on them, and a nearby lightning strike induces a surge on the wire. Without a discharge unit at the entrance, that energy rides the lead-in straight to the tuner, the TV, and whatever else shares the rack — and can arc inside the wall on the way. The unit bleeds the charge to ground at the door instead of letting it hunt for a path indoors.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer is one discharge unit for the whole antenna system, mounted wherever the lead-ins happen to end up — a distribution block in the attic, say. Section 810.20 wants a listed unit for each lead-in conductor, placed as near as practicable to the point of entrance. Second trap: assuming the factory grounding block on a satellite lead-in automatically qualifies. It serves only if it is listed for the discharge-unit role.

One discharge unit shared by two lead-in conductors — the section requires one for each lead-in.
Discharge unit mounted deep inside the attic run instead of as near as practicable to the point of entrance.
Discharge unit installed next to stored combustibles, or its ground landed on a convenient pipe instead of bonded per 810.21.
