sections.title: The antenna bonding and grounding recipe, (A) through (K)
sections.plain_explanation:
810.21 is the complete recipe for the conductors that bond an antenna mast and its discharge unit to ground — subsections (A) through (K).
• Material: copper, aluminum, copper-clad steel, bronze, or a similar corrosion-resistant conductive material. Copper-clad aluminum is not on the 810.21(A) list.
• The conductor may be solid or stranded, and it does not have to be insulated.
• Securely fastened in place, and protected where it is exposed to physical damage.
• Run in as straight a line as practicable, inside or outside the building.
• Landing: the intersystem bonding termination first, where one exists. Otherwise the nearest accessible point on the building grounding electrode system, or the other points the section lists.
• A building with no grounding means gets an electrode described in 250.52.
• Aluminum and copper-clad aluminum must not touch masonry or earth directly, and outdoors must not come within 18 in of the earth.
Conductor size and the bonding of separate electrodes get their own pages — 810.21(H) and 810.21(J) — because they are the two numbers inspectors actually measure.
sections.on_the_job: Gable-end mast on a Florida ranch home, dish and over-the-air antenna on the same mount. The crew runs 10 AWG copper — the 810.21(H) minimum — straight down the gable wall from the mast clamp, through a protective sleeve where the run passes the side walkway, and lands it on the intersystem bonding termination beside the meter. Total run 22 ft, no sharp bends, no attic tour. The termination was installed for exactly this conductor.

sections.why_it_exists: A mast and a lead-in are lightning collectors on the roof. The bonding conductor is the one planned path that carries a strike or a static charge to earth without side-flashing into the attic or the panel. Bends, corrosion and loose fastenings all raise the impedance of that path at exactly the moment it has to work, which is why the section reads like a recipe instead of a suggestion.

Conductor hanging loose down the wall, not securely fastened, with no protection where the mower and trimmer reach it.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer is copper-clad aluminum, picked because copper-clad steel is on the list and the two sound alike. They are not alike to the Code: copper-clad steel is a permitted 810.21(A) material; copper-clad aluminum is not named and is not permitted for this conductor.

sections.title: Antenna bonding conductor size — 10 AWG copper
sections.plain_explanation:
Section 810.21(H) sets the floor for the conductor that bonds an antenna mast or an antenna discharge unit to ground. It cannot be smaller than:
• 10 AWG copper
• 17 AWG copper-clad steel or bronze
• 8 AWG aluminum
The 17 AWG size looks impossibly thin until you know what it is: the messenger-style wire molded into the jacket of much satellite coax, copper-clad steel or bronze, which is why a factory dish lead-in can carry its own bond. Ten AWG copper is noticeably heavier than the 14 AWG floor for a communications protector bond in 800.100(A). That is deliberate — antennas sit up in the lightning, and the Code sizes their bond accordingly. The conductor itself follows the rest of 810.21: approved materials, securely fastened, protected from damage, and run as straight as practicable.
sections.on_the_job: On a Sharma house in Ocala, the dish and an over-the-air antenna share one mast. The bond is 10 AWG bare copper, run straight down the wall about 22 ft to the intersystem bonding termination at the Siemens meter-main. The dish lead-in arrived with the molded 17 AWG messenger, and it checked out as copper-clad steel, continuous to the grounding block — legal, but the 10 AWG run is still the one we pulled for the mast itself. If a helper reaches for the 14 AWG spool from the phone-protector work, stop him: that spool is for 800.100(A) bonds, not antennas.
sections.why_it_exists: A mast and a dish collect static charge and sit where lightning energy arrives first. The bond is the path that carries that energy to earth. A conductor that is too small can be damaged by the very surge it is supposed to drain, and a thin corroded wire can part without anyone noticing — leaving the discharge unit draining into air while the next surge looks for a path through the receiver and the house wiring instead.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer is 14 AWG, because 14 AWG is the Chapter 8 bonding floor everyone remembers. That floor belongs to 800.100(A), for protector and sheath bonds. Section 810.21(H) sets its own, heavier floor for antennas: 10 AWG copper. The second trap runs the other way — rejecting a 17 AWG messenger as too small to be legal. It is legal, but only as copper-clad steel or bronze, never as plain copper or copper-clad aluminum.
inspection_fails: Antenna mast bonded with 14 AWG copper — the 800.100(A) protector floor used where 810.21(H) requires 10 AWG copper.

Bonding conductor run with sharp bends and a long attic detour instead of as straight a line as practicable (810.21).
Separate ground rod driven at the dish and left unbonded to the power grounding electrode system — 810.21(J) requires a bond of at least 6 AWG copper.
Aluminum bonding conductor run in contact with the earth — 810.21 bars aluminum from earth and masonry contact and keeps it 18 in above the earth outdoors.

sections.title: Bonding a separate antenna electrode — 6 AWG again
sections.plain_explanation: If a separate ground rod or other electrode is installed to serve the radio and television equipment, it cannot stand alone. It must be bonded to the building's power grounding electrode system with a conductor no smaller than 6 AWG copper or the equivalent. This is the same anti-islanding rule as 800.100(D): one building, one earth reference, no matter how many systems drive their own rods. A separate electrode is permitted; a separate, unbonded electrode is a hazard wearing a ground rod's clothes.
sections.on_the_job: Driven a dish rod because the service was far away? The job ends when the 6 AWG bond ties it back to the power grounding system, not when the rod disappears below grade. Budget that conductor run when the dish location is chosen — on a wide Florida lot it is often the longest wire in the whole antenna job, and finding an unbonded rod on a service call means the original job was never finished.

sections.why_it_exists: Two electrodes that are not tied together do not sit at the same voltage. In a surge or a nearby lightning strike, thousands of volts can appear between them (800.100(D)) — and the equipment connected to both systems, or a person touching it, becomes the path that equalizes them. The 6 AWG bond keeps every rod at one reference so the difference never builds.
inspection_fails: Separate dish rod driven and left unbonded to the power grounding system.
Bond run made with a conductor smaller than 6 AWG copper.
Rod “grounded” to a hose bibb or an isolated pipe instead of the grounding electrode system.
sections.exam_trap: The trap: “A second rod makes the ground better, so bonding it back is optional — two grounds are better than one.” Wrong. An unbonded second rod is worse than none: it creates a second earth reference that can sit thousands of volts away from the first in a surge. 810.21(J) allows the rod only with the 6 AWG bond.

sections.title: Amateur and citizen-band transmitting stations
sections.plain_explanation:
Transmitting antennas for amateur (ham) and citizen-band stations get the receiving-station rules plus their own.
• Each outdoor antenna lead-in conductor needs an antenna discharge unit or another suitable means of draining static (810.57).
• The bonding and grounding conductors then follow 810.58: the protective bonding or grounding conductor must be at least as large as the lead-in and never smaller than 10 AWG copper, bronze, or copper-clad steel.
• The operating bonding or grounding conductor cannot be smaller than 14 AWG copper or its equivalent.
These stations also still owe the mast grounding of 810.15 and the installation rules of Part III of this article.
sections.on_the_job: Custom home in Ocala with a ham shack roughed into the garage. The owner runs a coax lead-in from a mast-mounted antenna to the shack. At the entrance we set a listed antenna discharge unit where the lead-in enters, run the protective bonding conductor in 10 AWG copper — never smaller than the lead-in — straight to the intersystem bonding termination at the Siemens meter-main, and run the operating bond in 14 AWG copper to the station ground bus. The mast itself is bonded under 810.15. One reference, one system: nothing in the shack floats at its own potential.

sections.why_it_exists: A transmitting antenna is a tall conductor in the sky, and it transmits: it couples real energy into whatever it touches. Wind builds static charge on the wire, and a nearby lightning strike can raise the lead-in to a dangerous voltage. The discharge unit bleeds that charge to ground before it reaches the radio, and the two bonding conductors keep the station's metal at one potential, so a fault or surge does not use the operator as the path.

sections.title: Article 820 — Community antenna television and radio distribution (coax)
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 820 covers coaxial cable systems that distribute television and radio signals — cable TV, and closed-circuit television of the same construction. The defining part of the system is the coax itself: a center conductor inside a metallic outer shield, and that shield is where this article's safety rules concentrate.
• The shield of a coax arriving from outside must be grounded at the entrance; the bonding and grounding conductor follows the recipe in 820.100.
• The cable types are listed in this article, and the general rules of Article 800 — separation, installation, fire — layer on top unless 820 changes them.
• No primary protector is required at a coax entrance, unlike a telephone circuit. If one is installed, it must be listed and applied at the entrance.
sections.on_the_job: For Sharma this is the cable company's drop, the grounding block on the side of the house, and the coax distribution inside. On a Marion Oaks spec house the block lands beside the Siemens meter-main: bond it there with 14 AWG copper, short and straight, to the intersystem bonding termination (820.100). Our scope is usually the bond at the block and clean, separated inside runs — the provider owns their drop up to the demarc, but the bond at our service is everybody's inspection item. Keep inside coax 2 in off power wiring in open runs (820.133).

sections.why_it_exists: The coax shield is a long metal path from the provider's plant straight into the house. Left ungrounded, it can carry lightning energy and fault voltage from outside plant to the television — and to anyone who touches the connector. Grounding the shield at the entrance gives that energy a path to earth before it gets inside, and it holds the shield at the same potential as the power system's ground, so the two systems never sit at different voltages.

The shield ground at the entrance is the requirement. A protector is optional, and if one is installed it must be listed.

sections.title: Grounding the coax shield at the point of entrance
sections.plain_explanation:
The outer conductive shield of a coaxial cable run to a building must be grounded as close as practicable to the point where the cable enters the building, following the conductor rules at 820.100.
• The connection can be made where the cable terminates outside the building, or just inside it. A grounded metal raceway can effectively extend the point of entrance — but 'as close as practicable' is the standard either way.
• The bond conductor is copper or another corrosion-resistant material, not smaller than 14 AWG, with capacity at least equal to the coax's outer shield — and never required to be larger than 6 AWG.
• At a one- or two-family dwelling the conductor runs as short as practicable and not more than 20 ft. Where that length cannot be met, a separate electrode may be installed and bonded back to the power grounding electrode system with 6 AWG or larger.
A coax shield left floating at a house is the single most common Chapter 8 defect in residential work.
sections.on_the_job: Coax rough-in on a Marion County spec house. The drop lands on the same wall as the Siemens meter-main, so set the grounding block within a few feet of the entrance hole and run the bond — 14 AWG copper is enough here — straight to the intersystem bonding termination. No coils, no scenic route. Land it before trim-out, then look at it again at trim: a block screwed to the wall with an empty ground lug is the classic write-up on this page. If the entrance is on the opposite wall from the service, measure the run before you pull it — over 20 ft at a one- or two-family dwelling means the separate-electrode route, bonded back with 6 AWG.

But the page sends the conductor rules to "820.100", while C8-840.93 sends the same rules to "800.100". After the 2020 Chapter 8 reorganization, the general bonding/grounding recipe lives in 800.100. Confirm whether 2020 820.100 still restates it or just references 800.100, then make both pages cite the same section.

sections.why_it_exists: The shield is the first part of the cable a surge meets. Lightning on the drop, a utility fault, or accidental contact with a power line puts voltage on that shield, and the shield runs straight indoors to the television and the modem. A short, solid bond at the entrance gives the energy a path into the grounding electrode system before it travels through the building. A floating shield does the opposite — it carries the surge inside and finds its own way out, usually through the equipment.

sections.title: Coax bonding and grounding conductors
sections.plain_explanation:
This section sends the coax shield's bonding and grounding conductor back to the same recipe as 800.100:
• Material: copper or another corrosion-resistant material.
• Size: no smaller than 14 AWG, with capacity at least equal to the coax's outer shield — but never required to exceed 6 AWG.
• Length at a house: in a one- or two-family dwelling, as short as practicable and no more than 20 ft. If that length cannot be met, a separate electrode may be installed and then bonded back to the power grounding electrode system with at least 6 AWG (820.100(D)).
• Systems that never leave the building: for coax isolated from outside plant, an exception allows the shield to be bonded through an equipment grounding conductor of a listed type instead.
sections.on_the_job: Same numbers as the phone protector, because the Code means them to rhyme: 14 AWG floor, 6 AWG ceiling, 20 ft at a house, 6 AWG bond for a separate rod. On a spec house, set the grounding block where the bond runs straight down to the intersystem bonding termination beside the meter-main — a 6 ft run, not a 25 ft tour of the garage. If the cable system is purely internal — a camera system that never exits — read the exception before driving anything. Otherwise, bond at the entrance like every other system in this chapter.

sections.title: Installing coaxial cable inside the building
sections.plain_explanation:
Listed coaxial cable inside a building follows the installation framework of Article 800 as this section applies it. Two rules drive the work:
• The cable type must match the space — plenum, riser, or general use — from this article's cable list: CATVP for plenums, CATVR for risers, CATV for general use, and CATVX for limited use in dwellings and raceways.
• Unlisted outside-plant coax may come into a building only a limited distance — 50 ft from the point of entrance — before listed cable is required, under 820.48. Past that point, the run must be listed coax of a type permitted for the space it passes through.
sections.on_the_job: Measure the entrance path on long custom homes: if the distribution panel sits more than 50 ft of cable run from where the drop enters, the whole run needs listed cable, not the provider's outdoor spool. In commercial ceilings and shafts, treat coax exactly like communications cable for fire rating — plenum type (CATVP) in plenums, CATVR riser cable between floors.

sections.why_it_exists: An outside-plant jacket is built for sun and water, not for fire. Run it deep into a building and it becomes fuel and smoke load in exactly the spaces people breathe from, and a path for flame to travel. The 50 ft limit caps how much of that unlisted jacket gets inside, and the type-for-space rules keep a fire on one floor from riding the coax to the next.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is measuring the 50 ft from the distribution panel, or as the crow flies. It is 50 ft of cable run from the point of entrance. The second trap is "listed is listed": a listed general-use CATV run through a plenum ceiling or up a riser shaft still fails — the type has to match the space.

sections.title: Separation for coaxial cable
sections.plain_explanation:
Coaxial cable obeys the same separation discipline as the rest of the chapter. Article 800's 800.133 states the general rule; this section carries it into the coax world, so a helper who learns one has learned both.
• Coax may not share a raceway or box with electric light and power conductors.
• Coax may not be supported from a raceway that contains power conductors.
• Coax keeps at least 2 in from light and power conductors — unless those conductors are in a raceway or in a sheathed cable assembly such as nonmetallic-sheathed, armored, or UF cable.
sections.on_the_job: Run coax in its own holes, on its own supports, 2 in off the power runs — the same muscle memory as Cat 6. The classic fail is a coax home-run bundle zip-tied along an EMT or draped over a Romex bundle in the attic. Separate supports cost minutes; a failed inspection costs a return trip.

sections.why_it_exists: Separation keeps a power fault from putting line voltage on a coax shield that a customer touches at the TV, and it keeps power-conductor heat and noise off the signal. It also keeps the two systems honest at inspection: a shared raceway hides which system a conductor belongs to, and coax strapped to a power raceway inherits every problem that raceway has.
sections.exam_trap: The trap runs both ways. "Coax can never come within 2 in of Romex" is wrong — nonmetallic-sheathed cable is a sheathed cable assembly, so the 2 in open-conductor separation is not what governs there. And "coax in the same conduit is fine if both are insulated" is always wrong: sharing a raceway with power conductors is prohibited outright.

sections.title: Where each coaxial cable type may be used — Table 820.154
sections.plain_explanation: Article 820 sorts coaxial cable into four listed types, and the ladder runs in one direction. CATVP, the plenum type, sits at the top; CATVR, the riser type, below it; then CATV, the general-purpose type; and CATVX, the limited-use type, at the bottom. Table 820.154 carries the substitution hierarchy: a higher type may be used in place of a lower one — plenum for riser, riser for general — and a lower type may never be substituted upward. Which type a given space demands is set by the article's installation and listing rules — not by the jacket color, and not by what the supplier shipped.
sections.on_the_job: Coax home runs through a return-air plenum in a light-commercial ceiling in Winter Park: CATVP, or a listed raceway — the CATV reel from the truck does not become legal because the ceiling is almost never opened. Before the pull, read the jacket legend on every reel and stage the plenum reels separately from the general-purpose stock.

In a riser shaft, a burning cable is a fuse that carries fire floor to floor. The ladder matches each cable's fire and smoke listing to the space, so a cable never becomes the path that spreads a fire.

sections.title: Coaxial cable types — CATVP, CATVR, CATV, CATVX
sections.plain_explanation: 820.179 lists the coaxial cable types and their markings. CATVP is the plenum type, CATVR the riser type, CATV the general-purpose type, and CATVX the limited-use type, restricted to dwellings and raceway. The substitution rule follows the chapter's pattern: a higher-listed type may be substituted for a lower one — plenum for riser, riser for general — and a lower type may never be substituted upward. The cable's voltage rating is not marked on the cable, so nobody mistakes coax for a power conductor. Read the print legend on the jacket; coax that carries no type marking carries no permission.
sections.on_the_job: CATVX is the trap type: fine in the dwelling work it is listed for, a violation pulled into a commercial riser. On a Winter Park strip-center rewire, the reel marked CATVX stays on the truck — the riser pulls get CATVR. Check the legend before the pull, not at the inspection.

sections.title: Article 830 — Network-powered broadband systems
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 830 covers broadband systems where the network itself sends the power: the provider's network powers the network interface unit at the customer's building, over the same plant that carries the signal. Because power arrives from off the premises on a communications cable, this article is stricter at the entrance than plain CATV:
• Its circuits get primary protection.
• Its shields, protectors, and interface-unit enclosures all get grounded.
The general rules of Article 800 still layer underneath, and 830 borrows the 800.100 grounding recipe for its conductors. Sharma meets 830 as the powered cable-broadband entrance on commercial and multi-dwelling work more than on single houses.
sections.on_the_job: Mid-rise condo in downtown Orlando: the cable provider's powered entrance lands in the telecom room, network interface units on the wall, powered from the street plant. Our scope stops at the demarc: we verify the primary protector is in place and the NIU enclosures and shields are grounded on the 800.100 recipe the article borrows. Recognize the powered entrance by the network interface unit and the provider's powering arrangement, not by the shape of the cable. Keep hands off the provider's powered plant beyond the demarc — that side is theirs.
sections.edition_note:
No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.why_it_exists: A plain communications cable brings signal; a network-powered broadband cable brings energy from a plant the building does not control, and it keeps bringing it during a building outage. Without primary protection and grounding at the entrance, a surge or fault on the provider's plant has a straight path into the customer's wiring and equipment. Article 830 exists to put the same entrance discipline on powered broadband that the older articles put on telephone and CATV.

sections.exam_trap: The trap is treating the powered broadband entrance like plain CATV under Article 820 because the cable looks the same. Wrong article. Where the network powers the interface unit, Article 830 governs: primary protection is required and the grounding follows the 800.100 recipe, not the CATV pages.

sections.title: Primary protectors on network-powered broadband circuits
sections.plain_explanation:
Because a network-powered broadband circuit brings both signal and network power in from outside plant, each of its conductors gets primary protection at the entrance, in the pattern of the protector rules used across this chapter (805.90):
• A listed primary protector — an arrester connected between each line conductor and ground.
• Mounted in, on, or immediately next to the building, as close as practicable to the point of entrance.
• Ahead of the network interface unit and the inside distribution.
The protector deals with the same two threats as at a telephone entrance: lightning energy riding in on the outside plant, and accidental contact between that plant and power conductors out on the poles.
sections.on_the_job: If a powered broadband entrance has no protector, treat it like a phone entrance with no protector: a provider-side correction to raise before the installation is signed off. On a Florida home or small office where the cable provider lands a network-powered drop, check the entrance before trim-out: protector present, ahead of the interface unit, and grounded — the shield, the protector, and the interface enclosure all land on the one building grounding reference (830.93). Sharma's part is usually the bond and the space: leave the protector accessible and its grounding path short and straight.

FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.why_it_exists: Outside plant is exposed plant. A lightning strike blocks away, or a fallen power conductor touching the drop, can put surge energy on a circuit that runs straight to equipment inside — and broadband circuits carry network power as well as signal. The protector gives that energy a path to ground at the door instead of through the building.

Second trap: mounting the protector after the interface unit; protection belongs at the point of entrance, ahead of it.

sections.title: Grounding shields, protectors, and the interface unit
sections.plain_explanation: Three things at a network-powered broadband entrance must be grounded: the metallic shield of the broadband cable, the primary protector, and the metallic enclosure of the network interface unit. Section 830.93 sends all three to the grounding conductor rules of 800.100 — the same rules that ground the other Chapter 8 systems. Everything metallic that the outside plant touches at the entrance ends up on the one building grounding reference: shield, protector ground, and enclosure alike. Bond only the shield and the job is two-thirds done; the enclosure is not optional. The grounding conductor itself follows 800.100 for size, routing and where it may land.
sections.on_the_job: New townhome rough-in, Kissimmee: the provider's coax lands on the primary protector at the garage demarc and the interface unit mounts beside it. Bond all three — shield, protector, enclosure — with 14 AWG minimum copper, run short and straight to the intersystem bonding termination, per 800.100. Photograph the entrance assembly at rough-in; broadband entrances get buried behind provider equipment fast, and the photo is your proof at final.

sections.why_it_exists: A broadband drop is a metal path from the outside plant straight into the building. Lightning and utility surges ride that path, and the protector can only dump energy it can reach ground with. Any metallic part left floating at the entrance — the enclosure is the one most often skipped — can sit at a dangerous voltage next to grounded equipment, waiting for a hand to bridge the gap.

sections.title: Broadband bonding and grounding conductors
sections.plain_explanation:
The bonding and grounding conductors for a network-powered broadband entrance follow the same dimensional rules as the rest of the chapter:
• Not smaller than 14 AWG, and not required to exceed 6 AWG.
• Run as short as practicable.
• Not more than 20 ft long in a one- or two-family dwelling.
The section carries the same escape hatch as 800.100 and 820.100: where the length cannot be met, a separate electrode is permitted, and the exception structure requires that electrode to be bonded back to the power grounding electrode system with a conductor of at least 6 AWG. By this point in the chapter the pattern should be familiar, because the Code intends it to be one pattern repeated.
sections.on_the_job: Cable broadband entrance on a two-family in Kissimmee: the provider's network interface unit lands on the garage wall, 12 ft of conductor run from the service. We run 14 AWG copper from the NIU ground lug straight to the intersystem bonding termination at the meter-main — inside the 20 ft dwelling limit, no upsizing needed. On a bigger commercial entrance where the run cannot stay short, the answer is not a longer skinny wire: it is a separate electrode at the entrance, bonded back to the power grounding electrode system with 6 AWG.

sections.why_it_exists: The bonding conductor is the path that drags a surge or a fault on the broadband plant down to the building's one grounding reference. A long, thin conductor has impedance that defeats it: the surge arrives faster than the path can carry it away, and the difference shows up as voltage between the cable plant and everything else in the house. Short, adequately sized, and bonded back is what keeps the potentials together.

sections.exam_trap: The trap is treating 6 AWG as the required size: "bonding conductors are 6 AWG." Wrong direction. 14 AWG is the minimum and the conductor is never required to exceed 6 AWG; 6 AWG is the size of the bond-back when a separate electrode is used because the length limit cannot be met.

sections.title: Separation for network-powered broadband cable
sections.figure_idea: Open-run cross-section: broadband cable held 2 in from a power run; raceway exception beside it.
sections.plain_explanation:
Broadband cable under Article 830 keeps the same separation discipline as the rest of Chapter 8.
• In a raceway, box, or enclosure, it does not run with electric light and power conductors except where 830.133's own conditions are met — a permanent barrier or listed divider between the two systems is the classic way those conditions are satisfied.
• In open runs, it keeps the chapter's familiar 2 in separation from power conductors.
• The 2 in is not required where one side or the other is in a raceway or a sheathed cable assembly, or where a continuous, firmly fixed nonconductor separates the two.
The network power on a broadband circuit makes the separation worth more, not less: this is the one communications-style cable whose network side arrives carrying power from outside the building.
sections.why_it_exists: Every other communications cable in the chapter is a guest in the building; a network-powered broadband cable arrives already energized from the network side. A cross-contact, a crushed jacket or a fault in a shared box can put that outside power — or building power — onto inside wiring and equipment that nobody expects to be live. Separation is the cheap, permanent insurance that the two systems never meet.
sections.on_the_job: Broadband entrance and inside runs: own holes, own supports, 2 in off the power runs — the same muscle memory as 800.133 and 820.133, because the Code intends one pattern for the whole chapter. On a Kissimmee rental rehab, the broadband drop crossed the garage ceiling 2 in clear of the open power runs; at the one place it had to cross the EMT feeder, the raceway itself satisfied the rule, so the crossing needed no extra spacing.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer is that broadband is 'just cable TV,' so it can share a box or raceway with power like any low-voltage cable. Wrong. It does not share a raceway, box or enclosure with power conductors except under 830.133's own conditions — and because the network side arrives carrying power, the separation matters more here, not less.

sections.title: Article 840 — Premises-powered broadband systems
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 840 covers broadband systems where the power is supplied at the premises instead of by the network. The classic case is fiber arriving at an optical network terminal — an ONT — that plugs into a local receptacle.
• The fiber itself carries no metallic path and no power, so there is no outside metallic shield arriving on glass.
• The protection focus shifts to any metallic members that do enter, and to the terminal equipment at the premises.
• The fiber cable itself follows the optical fiber rules of Article 770 in Chapter 7.
• Grounding questions go to the Chapter 8 pattern: the protector rules at 805.90 and the entrance bonding and grounding rules at 800.100, as the specific sections direct.
It is the shortest article in the chapter, and for Sharma it is mostly a fiber-to-the-home entrance on new custom work.

One census note, so nobody hunts for pages that do not exist: in NEC 2020 this chapter ends here. Chapter 8 has exactly six articles — 800, 805, 810, 820, 830 and 840 — and the article numbers 850 through 890 are not assigned in the 2020 edition. If a study aid or a newer book lists communications articles above 840, it is describing a different edition, and its section numbers will not match this one.
sections.on_the_job: Fiber-to-the-home on a new custom build: the provider mounts the ONT in the structured-wiring enclosure, and Sharma's scope is the premises side — a receptacle at the enclosure so the ONT plugs in where it lives, and a bond on the drop's metallic strength member at the entrance, run per 840.93. The glass itself gets no bond. Getting the receptacle location onto the rough-in plan is the whole game; after drywall it is a change order.

sections.why_it_exists: Network-powered systems push the protection problem out to the provider's plant. Premises-powered broadband brings live terminal equipment onto the customer's side of the entrance, fed from the building's own receptacles, while the drop can still carry metallic members in with it. Article 840 exists so that combination — local power, glass fiber, stray metal — gets its own entrance rules instead of borrowed ones.

sections.title: Grounding at a premises-powered broadband entrance
sections.plain_explanation:
Premises-powered broadband arrives at the building on a cable that may carry metallic members — a metallic shield, a strength member, or a similar conductive part. Where those members require grounding, 840.93 grounds them following the chapter's entrance-grounding pattern, as close as practicable to the point of entrance.
• The rule is about the metal in the cable, not the glass. All-dielectric fiber has nothing conductive to ground.
• The grounding conductor is the chapter's standard 800.100 recipe: copper or another corrosion-resistant conductive material.
• Not smaller than 14 AWG, and never required to be larger than 6 AWG.
• Run it as short as practicable — at a one- or two-family dwelling, not over 20 ft.
• If that length cannot be met, use a separate electrode and bond it back to the power grounding electrode system with 6 AWG, the 800.100(D) route.
Same numbers as the telephone and coax entrances, applied here to the metallic members that actually exist.
sections.on_the_job: New custom home, fiber-to-the-home: the provider's drop arrives at the ONT enclosure on the garage wall, and this drop carries a metallic strength member. Sharma's crew bonds that member at the entrance with 14 AWG copper, run 8 ft straight down to the intersystem bonding termination beside the Siemens meter-main — well inside the 20 ft dwelling limit. The next month, a second house gets an all-dielectric drop: no bond, and the job record says "all-dielectric drop, no metallic member," so nobody hunts for a missing bond later.

sections.why_it_exists: A metallic shield or strength member is a wire into the building from the pole or the pedestal. Lightning and utility surges ride it inside and look for a path to earth through whatever the cable touches — the terminal, the enclosure, a person. Grounding the member at the entrance gives that energy its path outside, before it reaches the equipment. Fiber itself carries light, not surges; the metal that travels with it is the hazard.

sections.title: Powering circuits — one cable carries the signal and the power
sections.plain_explanation:
Section 840.160 is titled 'Powering Circuits,' and it answers a narrow question: may a communications cable carry power as well as signal? Yes — with conditions:
• The cable is a listed communications cable (805.179), and the equipment it feeds is listed communications equipment (805.170)
• The power source is listed for the purpose (840.170(G))
• What the cable carries is power for communications equipment — this is not permission to put branch-circuit power on a communications cable
Where communications cables are substituted for Class 2 and Class 3 cables under 725.154(A), the installation must also comply with 725.144, the rules that keep power-and-data bundles from overheating. One exception: listed 4-pair cables where the rated current does not exceed 0.3 amperes in any conductor, 24 AWG or larger, do not have to comply with 725.144. The typical case is a 4-pair data cable carrying Ethernet and PoE-type power to a camera, a phone or an access point.
sections.on_the_job: Small Orlando office fit-out: a listed PoE switch in the rack feeds 14 ceiling cameras and access points over Cat 6. Each run is a listed 4-pair cable, the current per conductor sits well under the 0.3-ampere exception line, and the power source is the switch's own listed supply — the installation sits inside 840.160 without needing the 725.144 bundle calculation. The answer changes when the design grows: a fat bundle of powered runs, or communications cable substituted for Class 2 wiring, sends you to 725.144 and its table before you tie the bundle up.

sections.unverified_reason: Still unverified after Mike Holt recheck (2026-11-25): I believe 840.160 is titled 'Powering Circuits'. It permits communications cables to also carry circuits that power communications equipment, within power-limited limits. It is not a 'broadband-meets-light-and-power' separation exception as this page describes. I could not confirm the 2020 text first-hand. Pull the printed 2020 840.160 and rewrite the page from it; until then, do not publish the current interpretation.

sections.why_it_exists: Power on signal pairs is heat in a bundle. One cable carrying a fraction of an amp is nothing; dozens of powered cables tied tightly together can cook their own insulation, because the middle of the bundle cannot shed heat. The listing conditions and the 725.144 hook exist to keep the power inside what the cable system was tested to carry — and to keep 'powering' from becoming a back door for unlisted energy on a signal cable.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is reading 840.160 as a general permission to mix power and communications. It is not a separation exception, and it does not let a 120-volt branch circuit share a cable or a box with broadband drops. The permission runs the other way: listed communications cables may carry circuits that power communications equipment, from a listed source, inside the stated limits.
